title: Born Against, or why hobby programming communities are against LLM usage
titleZh: 天生反对，或者为什么业余编程社区反对使用 LLM
author: lladnar
relevanceReason: 命中 2 个 AI/科技关键词。
summaryRaw: I came across a GH thread related to chess engine development that made me think of why hobby programming communities are increasingly hostile toward LLM development. While the thread doesn’t give a lot of insight into answering the question, it prompted me to think about it a bit. I’ve seen similar sentiments expressed in other niche hobby programming communities like OSDev, LangDev, TxtDev, EmuDev, RLDev, the demoscene, and code golfers. The general consensus seems to be that the knowledge that these communities work in is hard-fought and the use of LLMs is a form of missing the point entirely. In these communities (keep in mind that there is an implicit “not all…” throughout) the process of mastering a difficult field itself is the product, and something that runs is generally a nice-to-have. Further, I’ve noticed that even in the instances where there was earnest early engagement with LLMs in some of these niche communities, the well was quickly poisoned by a combination of a lack of a deep understanding by the LLM practitioners, and a vitriolic subset of those communities that view the LLM enterprise as a form of cheating. Granted these communities have, in general, historically been characterized by feverish gatekeeping and painstakingly slow progress, so it makes sense that there might be a desire to grab some easy cachet by bursting onto the scene like the Kool-Aid man. OH YEAH…. OH NO! In traditional niche dev circles, respect is earned slowly through years of activity in their respective fora, sharing elegant code, displays of genuine curiosity, and through sharing deep domain knowledge along the way. At the end of the day, these communities don’t care if your code works at all, but instead care that you know why and how it works. To me, an LLM functions best as a force multiplier, not a surrogate. In the hands of an expert who already understands a domain deeply, it could act like a lever.1 But in these niche communities, the entire exercise is in the learning. Using an LLM to generate the finished piece doesn’t make us craftsmen; it just robs us of the craft. :F This is the latest in my evolving thoughts on LLMs. Also see: LLMe and Mind the van Emden Gap
That said, expertise offers no natural immunity against being fooled by LLMs.↩︎

comments.author: alkonaut
comments.textRawHtml:
Programming has five phases effectively:

1) You figure out what problem to solve.

2) You figure out HOW to solve the problem.

3) You actually implement the solution.

4) You see the solution work, for yourself.

5) You ship/deploy/publish the program. This means you see people be happy users and/or you get paid for it and so on.

If you're an entrepreneur type, you probably enjoy the first and last steps most, and you see steps 2-4 as mostly a chore. If you're a tinkerer, you don't care much for 1 and 5, and you see 2-4 as the whole point of programming. I'm a tinkerer. I'd be happy to just write code and throw it away. Coding is like solving sudokus. I could skip steps 1 and 5 forever. I don't ever need to show any code to anyone. In fact, most of the time when programming I do steps 2 and 3 and even skip 4. I don't even finish! I work weeks on something until I lose interest, and I know that in order to even run it, it would be several more weeks. A PoC is enough. Or just a half one. It's just code-to-structure-thoughts, not to create anything finished.

The 5 phases look kind of symmetric. The outermost layer (1 and 5) are the entrepreneurial steps. If you're a product owner or CEO, you might work strictly at steps 1,5. Then steps 2-4 are the managerial/architectural steps. If you're a very senior IC at a large company, you might work at this level, without actually doing much coding. Only the inner most step (3) is the manual creation of source code. Even though it's 5 different phases, it's just "3 layers" of programming.

The problem as I see it is that I enjoy step 3. And LLMs are good at step 3 almost exclusively. So they just pick the best bit of this dish, and leave me with the rest.

If you're an entrepreneurial type, the LLM appears to take the _worst_ bit of the work from you. Great.
comments.textZhHtml:
编程有效地分为五个阶段：

1) 您弄清楚要解决什么问题。

2) 您弄清楚如何解决问题。

3) 您实际实现解决方案。

4) 您自己看到解决方案有效。

5) 您交付/部署/发布程序。这意味着您看到人们成为快乐的用户和/或您因此获得报酬等等。

如果您是企业家类型，您可能最喜欢第一步和最后一步，并且您认为步骤 2-4 主要是一件苦差事。如果您是一位修补匠，那么您不太关心 1 和 5，并且您将 2-4 视为编程的全部要点。我是一个修补匠。我很乐意只写代码然后把它扔掉。编码就像解决数独一样。我可以永远跳过步骤 1 和 5。我不需要向任何人展示任何代码。事实上，大多数时候我在编程时都会执行步骤 2 和 3，甚至跳过 4。我什至没有完成！我在某件事上工作了数周，直到失去兴趣，而且我知道为了运行它，还需要几周的时间。一个 PoC 就足够了。或者只是半个。这只是代码到结构的想法，而不是创建任何完成的东西。

这 5 个阶段看起来有点对称。最外层（1 和 5）是创业步骤。如果您是产品负责人或首席执行官，您可能会严格按照步骤 1,5 进行工作。然后步骤 2-4 是管理/架构步骤。如果您是一家大公司的高级 IC，您可能会从事此级别的工作，而无需实际进行大量编码。只有最里面的步骤（3）是手动创建源代码。尽管它有 5 个不同的阶段，但它只是编程的“3 层”。

我看到的问题是我喜欢第 3 步。法学硕士几乎只擅长第 3 步。所以他们只是挑选这道菜中最好的部分，然后把剩下的留给我。

如果你是企业家类型，法学硕士似乎会从你身上夺走最差的部分。太棒了。

children.author: shiomiru
children.textRawHtml:
There's also the economic problem that programmers had until recently been highly regarded because steps 2-3 were hard. "Open source" solved this partially by utilizing the labor such (relatively) well-paid people gave away "for the love of it", but it was not nearly enough to put most out of work.

Now there is a plagiarism machine built on top of decades of this work that seemingly solves 3 and promises to solve 2 (badly, but usually this matters little), the programmers that (indirectly) helped build it are told they're fools for doing so, and threatened by losing their status if they don't adapt to the "entrepreneurial way" (well, the full promise is "you'll lose it anyway, but if you cooperate in stuffing sama's pockets then maybe you get to keep it a bit longer").

So what really surprises me is not that people are upset but that so few are.
children.textZhHtml:
还有一个经济问题，程序员直到最近才受到高度重视，因为步骤 2-3 很困难。 “开源”通过利用这些（相对）高薪的人们“因为热爱”而放弃的劳动力部分地解决了这个问题，但这还不足以让大多数人失业。

现在有一个抄袭机器建立在数十年的这项工作之上，看似解决了 3 并承诺解决 2（糟糕，但通常这无关紧要），（间接）帮助构建它的程序员被告知他们这样做是愚蠢的， 并且如果他们不适应“创业方式”，就会受到失去地位的威胁（好吧，完整的承诺是“无论如何你都会失去它，但如果你配合塞满大人的口袋，那么也许你可以保持更长的时间”）。

所以真正让我惊讶的不是人们感到不安，而是很少有人感到不安。

children.author: Tade0
children.textRawHtml:
I'm not concerned. Never in my life have I experienced stakeholders just going "hmm, yes - this is enough software for our purposes - we won't be needing your services any more".

There's always another feature that can be implemented or a new problem to be solved. Tools only ever accelerated the pace at which we were able to follow this insatiable hunger for more software.

Right now people are getting fired left and right because all the money that used to be spent on staff now goes to build more data centers and also because cutting corporate expenses is in vogue now.

This too shall pass and with demographics as they are and young people getting discouraged from pursuing this field I believe long term my position is safe.

Also a huge chunk of what AI company CEOs say is just pure bullshit that they only say because they need that sweet, sweet investor money. Bullshit writes a check that eventually must be cashed.
children.textZhHtml:
我不担心。在我的一生中，我从未经历过利益相关者只是说“嗯，是的 - 这对于我们的目的来说已经足够了 - 我们不再需要您的服务”。

总是有另一个可以实现的功能或有一个新的问题需要解决。工具只会加快我们追随对更多软件的永不满足的渴望的步伐。

现在，人们正在被解雇，因为过去花在员工身上的所有钱现在都花在了建设更多的数据中心上，也因为现在流行削减公司开支。

这也会过去，随着人口结构的变化，年轻人对这个领域的追求感到沮丧，我相信从长远来看，我的职位是安全的。

还有很大一部分人工智能公司首席执行官所说的纯粹是废话，他们只是因为需要投资者的资金而说这些。 Bullshit 写了一张最终必须兑现的支票。

children.author: barbazoo
children.textRawHtml:
I can imagine that this will lead to an explosion in software where we didn't see software before. Much smaller business now have the ability to build something themselves, not with a team of highly paid software developers but a single programmer maune.

Big business is going to struggle with building software for a while. Writing code is often not the hard part there already, coordination, larger understanding of the system is I think.
children.textZhHtml:
我可以想象，这将导致我们以前从未见过的软件爆炸式增长。规模小得多的企业现在有能力自己构建一些东西，而不是通过高薪软件开发人员团队，而是通过一个程序员 maune。

大企业将在一段时间内为构建软件而苦苦挣扎。我认为，编写代码通常并不是困难的部分，协调、对系统的更大理解才是。

children.author: Tade0
children.textRawHtml: My cowork buddy is living this reality - he's an independent analyst and previously he needed to shell out significant cash to have certain scripts (largely scrapers, social media API integration etc.) done, now it's all just a prompt away.
children.textZhHtml: 我的同事就生活在这个现实中 - 他是一名独立分析师，之前他需要花费大量现金才能完成某些脚本（主要是抓取工具、社交媒体 API 集成等），现在这一切都只需一个提示即可。

children.author: barbazoo
children.textRawHtml: I love it. It makes me feel like I have super powers. I wish it wasn't so resource intensive.
children.textZhHtml: 我喜欢它。这让我感觉自己拥有超能力。我希望它不是那么资源密集型。

children.author: stronglikedan
children.textRawHtml:
> Right now people are getting fired left and right

FWIW, it's just a few large companies laying off large groups, not so much people getting fired left and right at a lot of companies. What is happening at a lot of companies is that they aren't hiring juniors, because, why would you when LLMs are cheaper and fill that role perfectly (if you actually treat them like juniors).
children.textZhHtml:
> 现在人们左右被解雇

FWIW，只是少数大公司大规模裁员，而不是很多公司左右被解雇的人。很多公司的情况是他们不雇用初级员工，因为，当法学硕士更便宜并且可以完美地填补这个职位时，你为什么要雇用初级人才（如果你实际上像对待后辈一样对待他们）。

children.author: crooked-v
children.textRawHtml: Also, give it another couple of years and there's going to be a lot of work for any moderately experienced developer fixing broken slopcode hitting the hard wall of bad design.
children.textZhHtml: 此外，再过几年，对于任何经验丰富的开发人员来说，修复损坏的 slopcode 会遇到不良设计的难题，这将需要做大量的工作。

children.author: pigpop
children.textRawHtml: Maybe I'm just old but people talking about being in programming for "status" or to be "highly regarded" really irks me. I'd rather see the entire field burnt to the ground and replaced by robots than to have it become a status profession like lawyering.
children.textZhHtml: 也许我只是老了，但人们谈论编程是为了“地位”或“受到高度重视”，这真的让我很恼火。我宁愿看到整个领域被夷为平地并被机器人取代，也不愿让它成为像律师一样有地位的职业。

children.author: rayiner
children.textRawHtml: Having done both, lots of lawyers are also nerds who just like to tinker with the law and words. Often very well paid tinkering, but that's true for programmers as well.
children.textZhHtml: 在完成这两件事后，很多律师也是书呆子，他们只是喜欢修改法律和文字。通常修补工作的报酬很高，但对于程序员来说也是如此。

children.author: pigpop
children.textRawHtml: I don't disagree. You can add medical doctors to the list as well, lots of nerds but also a lot of clout chasers and money-grubbers who couldn't care less about the profession. I don't want to see programming take the same path.
children.textZhHtml: 我不同意。你也可以将医生添加到名单中，其中有很多书呆子，但也有很多不关心这个职业的影响力追逐者和贪图金钱的人。我不想看到编程走同样的路。

children.author: ambicapter
children.textRawHtml: It already has? Clout-chasers and money grubbers go for all the big tech jobs in droves.
children.textZhHtml: 已经有了？追逐影响力和贪图金钱的人成群结队地争夺所有大型科技工作。

children.author: hunterpayne
children.textRawHtml: And its been that way for at least a decade.
children.textZhHtml: 这种情况至少持续了十年。

children.author: dctoedt
children.textRawHtml:
> Having done both [software and law], lots of lawyers are also nerds who just like to tinker with the law and words

Having also done both: In legal drafting work, there's less systematic pre-release testing before the equivalent of a "program" is loosed upon the world. There's not much in the way of counterparts to software unit testing and regression testing, in part because legal-drafting clients can be vociferous in demanding that their lawyers keep costs down.

Lawyers who like to tinker with words can fuck things up more often and at greater scale — e.g., by inflicting compulsory burdens and costs on others — than can most programmers. That includes, e.g., contract drafters and litigation counsel, plus lobbyists trying to influence draft legislation and regulations.

I'm not-infrequently dismayed by the quality of the contracts I review for clients because of the "tinkering with words" by the lawyers on the other side of the deal. Back when I did IP litigation, I was sometimes likewise dismayed by the bullshit arguments that some lawyers felt free to make in their court papers because what the hell, the worst that can happen is almost never more than the judge just saying "no." And as mostly a law professor these days, I review court opinions all the time and am regularly amazed how judges (and their law clerks, such as Rayiner used to be) can be so patient in responding to such arguments.
children.textZhHtml:
> 既做了[软件和法律]，很多律师也是书呆子，只是喜欢摆弄法律和文字

也做了两件事：在法律起草工作中，在相当于“程序”的东西发布到世界各地之前，没有那么系统的发布前测试。软件单元测试和回归测试的对应方式并不多，部分原因是法律起草客户可能会大声要求他们的律师降低成本。

喜欢修补文字的律师可能会比大多数程序员更频繁、更大规模地把事情搞砸——例如，通过给他人带来强制性的负担和成本。其中包括合同起草者和诉讼律师，以及试图影响立法和法规草案的游说者。

我经常对我为客户审查的合同质量感到沮丧，因为交易另一方的律师“修改文字”。当我进行知识产权诉讼时，我有时也会对一些律师在法庭文件中随意提出的废话论点感到沮丧，因为到底是什么，可能发生的最糟糕的情况几乎永远不会比法官只是说“不”更重要。如今，作为一名法学教授，我一直在审查法庭意见，并且经常惊讶于法官（以及他们的法律助理，例如以前的雷纳）如何如此耐心地回应此类论点。

children.author: rayiner
children.textRawHtml:
> Having also done both: In legal drafting work, there's less systematic pre-release testing before the equivalent of a "program" is loosed upon the world. There's not much in the way of counterparts to software unit testing and regression testing, in part because legal-drafting clients can be vociferous in demanding that their lawyers keep costs down.

Yeah, at least in litigation you get relatively immediate feedback in the form of a decision. Seems anxiety inducing to me to draft these contracts and have no feedback loop unless something blows up years later.
children.textZhHtml:
> 同时完成了这两件事：在法律起草工作中，在相当于“程序”的版本发布到世界各地之前，系统性的预发布测试较少。软件单元测试和回归测试的对应方式并不多，部分原因是法律起草客户可能会大声要求他们的律师降低成本。

是的，至少在诉讼中，你会以决定的形式获得相对即时的反馈。似乎焦虑促使我起草这些合同，并且没有反馈循环，除非几年后出现问题。

children.author: shiomiru
children.textRawHtml:
I meant it as an euphemism for "it's universally sought after (i.e., you'll probably find a job)". Few would think being a programmer gives you some kind of special "social status"; it's always been a "nerd" hobby that happened to pay (relatively) well.

(I guess by now you have a solid retirement plan; maybe if the field had been burnt to the ground while you were younger, you'd have had a different opinion.)
children.textZhHtml:
我的意思是“它受到普遍追捧（即，你可能会找到一份工作）”的委婉说法。 很少有人会认为成为一名程序员会给你某种特殊的“社会地位”；这一直是一种“书呆子”的爱好，碰巧报酬（相对）不错。

（我想现在你已经有了一个可靠的退休计划；也许如果你年轻时这个领域被烧毁了，你会有不同的看法。）

children.author: ModernMech
children.textRawHtml: Being a good programmer gives you special social status amongst people who value programming. You only have to look at how people talk about others as slop coders and seek to expand their coding reputations. Those people are the most threatened by AI because of how it implicates their carefully crafted personas as coding gurus and keepers of knowledge.
children.textZhHtml: 成为一名优秀的程序员可以让您在重视编程的人中拥有特殊的社会地位。你只需要看看人们如何谈论其他人是垃圾编码员，并寻求扩大他们的编码声誉。这些人受到人工智能的威胁最大，因为人工智能让他们精心打造的角色成为编码大师和知识的守护者。

children.author: SoftTalker
children.textRawHtml: It also gives you a special social status amongst people who do not understand programming: nobody wants to talk to you, at least not about your job.
children.textZhHtml: 它还为您在不懂编程的人中提供了特殊的社会地位：没有人愿意与您交谈，至少不想谈论您的工作。

children.author: bananaflag
children.textRawHtml:
Could you elaborate?

I think back in the 90s when I was a teenager I thought it to be a good thing that there is a rise in status for a class of people characterized by clear thinking.
children.textZhHtml:
您能详细说明一下吗？

我想起来，在90年代，当我十几岁的时候，我认为以清晰思维为特征的一类人的地位上升是一件好事。

children.author: embedding-shape
children.textRawHtml: The older I get, the more I realize how many problems in society is because there are different "classes" of people. The more we can eschew that, the better it becomes for most people. While yes, I also see myself as having "clearer thinking" than many people , maybe because of the thousands of hours building and maintaining software, I'm not of the impression that my life deserves a higher status than others merely because of this. It's not "they think right and they think wrong", it's just "everyone thinks differently, but it's all valid thinking".
children.textZhHtml: 随着年龄的增长，我越发意识到社会上有多少问题是因为人有不同的“阶层”。我们越能避免这种情况，对大多数人来说就越好。虽然是的，我也认为自己比许多人有“更清晰的思维”，也许是因为花费了数千个小时构建和维护软件，我并不认为仅仅因为这个我的生活就应该比其他人更高的地位。不是“他们认为对，他们认为错”，只是“每个人的想法不同，但都是有效的想法”。
